A roost is a place where birds — and sometimes bats — go to sleep, rest, or take shelter, especially at night. Think of it as a bird's bedroom, or its regular sleeping spot.

Just as you have a bed you return to each night, a bird has its roost — a specific place it comes back to when the day ends.

A roost isn't one fixed thing. It's wherever birds regularly settle down together to sleep. It could be:

  • A branch (or cluster of branches) in a tree
  • A ledge, beam, or wooden bar inside a henhouse or barn
  • A rocky cliff face
  • Any elevated, sheltered spot birds consistently return to for the night

The key idea is that it's a regular, familiar resting place — not just any random spot a bird lands on briefly.
The two things "roost" can refer to

The word "roost" (as a noun) carries two closely related meanings, and both are common:

1. The physical place itself
This is the spot — the branch, the ledge, the structure — where birds sleep.
Example: "The pigeons flew back to their roost under the bridge as the sun went down."

2. The gathering of birds at that place
"Roost" can also refer to the entire group of birds that share and occupy that sleeping spot together.
Example: "A roost of starlings settled noisily into the trees."

Both senses are correct. Context usually makes it obvious which one is meant.
When and why birds use a roost

Birds typically return to their roost at dusk and leave at dawn. The roost serves several purposes for them: protection from predators during the night (height and shelter help), warmth (birds huddled together retain body heat), and a sense of safety in a familiar, trusted place.

Some birds roost alone; many others — like starlings, crows, and pigeons — roost in enormous communal groups, sometimes numbering in the thousands. These mass gatherings are also called roosts.

The word appears in two very common expressions in English. These are worth knowing because you'll encounter them often:

1. "Rule the roost"
This idiom means to be the dominant person — the one in charge, the one who makes decisions in a household, group, or organization.
Example: "In that house, the grandmother rules the roost."
The image comes from the dominant hen (or rooster) in a henhouse controlling the other birds at the roost.

2. "Chickens come home to roost"
This expression means that the negative consequences of your past actions eventually catch up with you. Just as chickens always return to their roost at night, your mistakes always find their way back to you.
Example: "He cut corners for years, and now the chickens have come home to roost — the whole project is falling apart."

Where it can beA branch, ledge, beam, cliff — any sheltered spot birds return to

The simplest way to hold onto this word: a roost is to a bird what a bed is to a person — the familiar, trusted place you return to at the end of the day to sleep.
